Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

take something hard verb

also take it hard, take it badly, be upset by, take this hard, resent, take to heart

classical

Cic. Tusc. 4.17.40: aegrē ferre repulsam cōnsulātūs (Lewis & Short), s.v. ferō
Traupman 325

aegrē ferre

ferō with the adverb aegrē; the thing as object, or the accusative and infinitive

take badly, be upset by

Also molestē ferre and, more strongly, graviter ferre.

Other words

  • dūrum accipere — take as hard

    also used · modern · Traupman 100: hoc dūrum accipiō; Traupman 325

    Traupman’s phrase. Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase.

  • graviter ferre (+ acc. & inf.) — take it hard that, be upset that

    also used · classical · Cic. Verr. 2.1.152: hoc ēreptum esse, graviter et acerbē ferre (Lewis & Short s.v. ferō); Traupman 389

  • cordī habēre — take to heart

    also used · modern · Traupman 327

    Classically cordī esse is to be dear to someone, to please (quod tibi magnopere cordī est, Lucil., Lewis & Short s.v. cor); we have found no classical instance of cordī habēre for “take to heart”.

See also I’m sorry.

SourcesLewis & Short: aegre · Lewis & Short: fero

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
